1:
Whether Abram was called once or twice is the first question, and Clarke says plainly that there is great dissension about it. He follows Hales for two calls, the first omitted in the Old Testament but recorded in the speech of Stephen, where the God of glory appears in Mesopotamia before Abram dwelt in Charran, and the second recorded only here; and he rests part of the case on the tense, that the Lord said rather than had said. Gill also allows two appearances, reporting Aben Ezra for the earlier at Ur and Jarchi for a later one at Haran after Terah's death, and thinks the same words or very near the same were spoken on both occasions. Calvin argues for one call only, and argues it hard: if Abram were already without a country and sojourning elsewhere, the command to depart from his land and his father's house would have been superfluous; Stephen testifies that God appeared to him before Charran; and the later word about the Lord who brought him out of Ur points the same way. Ellicott settles the tense against the tradition, since the Hebrew reads simply and Jehovah said.

Ellicott adds that the phrase thy country proves Abram and his father were no new settlers at Ur but a family long established there, and observes that the narrative is not beginning afresh here but reverting to its own starting point after sketching the family. Calvin makes the same continuity a moral point by joining the sentence to the close of the previous chapter, and rules out four ordinary motives for emigration in a row: Terah and Abram were not impelled by levity as rash and fickle men are, nor drawn away by disgust with their own country as morose persons often are, nor fugitives on account of crime, nor led by any foolish hope, since Abram did not move a foot except as he was guided. He adds that God could not have spoken so except to a man settled in his nest, his affairs unshaken, living quietly among his relatives. Keil and Delitzsch state the shape of the word itself, that it contained a command and a promise together, and that what Abram was to leave was everything — his country, his kindred, his father's house. Henry finds the design double, to try his faith and obedience and to set him apart.

Calvin explains why a promise is annexed to the command at all, and for him it is not decoration: we are slothful to obey, so the Lord would command in vain unless we were animated by a superadded confidence in his grace, faith being unable to stand except on the promises and obedience being produced by faith alone. Wesley reads the promise of a great nation as both relief and trial at once, relief because Abram's burden was that he had no child, and trial because his wife had long been barren, so that if he believed it must be against hope, his faith building on the power that can raise up children out of stones. Gill divides the nation into a literal one, the people descended from him, and a spiritual one of believers in every nation who walk in the steps of his faith. Clarke hears the promise of a great name pointing forward to the change from a high father to the father of a multitude. Calvin then finds in the blessing and cursing the accustomed form of covenants between kings, who promise each other the same friends and the same enemies, and calls it an inestimable pledge that God should so condescend.
4:
Henry makes the obedience the whole point of the verse: Abram was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, and his obedience was speedy and without delay, submissive and without dispute, since he went out not knowing whither he went but knowing whom he followed. He notes the age as an aggravation of the same virtue, seventy-five being a time when a man should rather have rest and settlement, so that here is an instance of an old convert. Calvin uses the verse to close the earlier argument, since those who put the call at Charran lay hold of these words; he answers that Moses, having given the cause of the departure, is simply returning to the thread of his history, and confesses he does not know why Abram lingered there at all unless God laid a hand on him to delay the sight of the land. Ellicott supplies the likelier reason, that Abram stayed only on his father's account and resumed the journey at his death. Clarke turns to arithmetic instead, reckoning from the two ages that Terah was a hundred and thirty when Abram was born, so that the seventieth year named earlier belongs to Haran.

The souls they had gotten in Haran divide the corpus cleanly. Wesley takes them for proselytes whom Abram had persuaded to worship the true God and to go with him, and borrows a rabbi's phrase for it, souls gathered under the wings of the divine Majesty. Clarke allows either reading, that the phrase may cover the persons employed in Abram's service or the persons he had been the instrument of converting, and notes that the Chaldee paraphrasts took the second. Ellicott reports the same Jewish tradition and grants that such converts may have been in the company, but holds that most were dependents and slaves, with the caution that our word slave suggests a relation very unlike the one that actually existed. Keil and Delitzsch give no ground at all, ruling that these are not souls whom they had begotten but the male and female slaves that Abram and Lot had acquired. Calvin agrees on the meaning and then stops on it, remarking that this is the first mention of servitude in the Scriptures. Gill leaves the servants aside to note that Sarai and Lot came willingly, she on the score of religion as well as of marriage.

Calvin turns that remark into the longest reflection in the passage. From the first mention of servitude he infers that not long after the deluge the wickedness of man caused liberty, which by nature was common to all, to perish for a great part of mankind; where it originated he thinks hard to determine, unless by the common opinion that it arose from wars, conquerors compelling those taken in battle to serve them, from which the very name of bondman is derived; but whether the first slaves were subjugated by the laws of war or reduced to it by want, he holds it certain that the order of nature was violently infringed, since men were created to cultivate mutual society with one another. Ellicott attends to the property instead and draws an inference from it: the substance was not cattle only but wealth of every kind, and since Abram was very rich in silver and gold he had apparently engaged in trade during the years at the first halting place, and so may have known the routes the caravans took. Clarke describes what they were travelling toward, a good land possessed by a bad people who for their iniquities were to be expelled.
6:
Ellicott begins from the ground itself, since Shechem means shoulder and named the ridge joining Ebal and Gerizim, a name taken from the natural conformation and so possibly very ancient; the modern Nablous is a worn-down Flavia Neapolis, and he cites a traveller's description of the valley as an oasis of remarkable beauty set like Damascus in a desert and girt with barren mountains. Clarke corrects the next word, since the term rendered plain should be oak, the Septuagint giving the lofty oak, so that the place was likely known for a grove of them or for one of stupendous bulk. On the notice that the Canaanite was then in the land he refuses the usual inference: this is thought an interpolation, on the ground that the words must have been written after the expulsion under Joshua, but Moses states only that at the time Abram passed through the land was inhabited by Canaan's descendants, which involves neither contradiction nor absurdity. Henry finds in the same clause how little comfort Abram had, arriving without observation where he might have expected the kings of Canaan to surrender their crowns, and reckoning that he could not have ground to pitch his tent on but by their permission.

Ellicott marks the appearance as a first of its kind, since until now the communications between God and man had been direct and without any visible medium, God commanding Adam, calling him, saying unto Cain and unto Noah; from this point a visible manifestation recurs, and is later connected with the phrase an angel of Jehovah. Clarke notes the same novelty by way of the man, that Abram is the first to whom God is said to have shown himself, in Ur and now at the oak, and suggests the tree may have been called the teacher's oak because God instructed Abram there about the future possession of the land. Gill and Clarke both suppose the form to have been that of the Son. Keil and Delitzsch read the altar as the point of the whole verse, the appearance marking this land as henceforth the scene of Jehovah's manifestation, which Abram understood, so that he made the hallowed soil a place for the worship of the God who had appeared. Calvin observes what the help actually consisted of, a bare word offered to a childless old man with a barren wife, insipid consolation to the flesh though faith has a different taste.

The removals themselves are read as a discipline. Calvin counts three within a short period and denies Abram ran hither and thither for his own gratification like light-minded persons, holding that necessities drove him out to teach him by continual habit that he was not merely a stranger but a wanderer in the land of which he was lord; and he draws the reproof, that if Abram bore his wanderings patiently our fastidiousness is inexcusable when we murmur at not being granted a quiet nest. Ellicott sees no need to look for a special reason at all, since breaking camp was the usual condition of nomad life and Abram's wealth in cattle would force frequent changes. Keil and Delitzsch agree he moved for pasture, and fix the site precisely, with Ai to the east and Bethel to the west, the name Bethel used ahead of its time since the place was still called Luz. Clarke turns the altar into a rule for householders, that where Abram has a tent God must have an altar, and asks how few who build houses ever think of the necessity of building one. Gill measures the distance from Sichem at about twenty miles.
10:
The famine is taken by everyone as a trial rather than an accident, and they differ only in what it tried. Henry sets out two things it tested at once, what Abram would think of the God who brought him there, since nothing short of a strong faith could keep up good thoughts of him under such a providence, and what he would think of the land of promise, whether the grant of it were worth accepting in exchange for the country he had left. Calvin sharpens the same point by recalling the fertility Abram was used to, first in Chaldea and then at Charran where he plainly prospered, so that being now driven out by hunger from the very land in which he had promised himself abundance was a temptation to the quick. Clarke notes that this is the first famine on record and that it fell on the most fertile land then under the sun. Ellicott turns instead to the mechanics, that rain falls in Palestine at only two seasons so the failure of either would be felt at once, especially in a dry region, while Egypt is watered by the flooding of the Nile from Abyssinian rains and so probably had not suffered.

Ellicott also uses the famine to date the episode, since Abram was seventy-five on leaving Haran and Ishmael was thirteen when his father was ninety-nine, which leaves only about eight years for everything recorded between; the famine must therefore have fallen within a few years of the arrival. On what Abram then did the corpus turns sharply critical, and does not spare him. Calvin calls the place a rock on which many strike and weighs the case in both directions: there is something of falsehood mixed with the dissimulation he presses on his wife, and though Abram afterwards pleads that he feigned nothing untrue, he was greatly culpable in this, that by concealing the marriage he stripped her chastity of its legitimate defence, and it was no doing of his that she was not prostituted. Gill grants that calling her a sister was not a direct lie, since she was his sister in a sense, but holds it was meant to conceal the truth and endangered her, showing distrust of divine protection, so that the best of men are liable to sin and the strongest believer to fall. Clarke puts it as suppressing part of the truth rather than telling an untruth.

Ellicott states the objection in its exact form, that the words were true literally, Sarai being Terah's daughter, yet absolutely false, since they implied she was wholly his sister and therefore not his wife. Clarke supplies the relationship from the later chapter, a sister by the same father and a different mother, and reports without endorsing the conjecture that she was rather Haran's daughter and so Terah's grandchild, which he thinks lacks probability enough to stand. He is also interested in why the danger existed, judging that Sarai's complexion differed widely from the swarthy Egyptians and would therefore be the more coveted, and that Abram supposed they would not scruple to kill a husband to gain undisturbed possession of a wife; he notes that commentators cannot agree on her age, some making her ninety and others sixty-five, and works the second figure out from the ten years between the pair. Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole Egyptian passage as a second lesson matching the first, since the famine in Canaan was to teach Abram that even in the promised land food comes from the Lord, while Egypt was to teach him that earthly craft is soon put to shame. Wesley asks what will become of the willows when the cedars are so shaken.
14:
Ellicott sets the episode in a history the other commentators do not reach for. In Abram's day Canaan was the highway into Egypt, and Semitic immigration was heavy enough to overspread the Delta and at length, under the name of the Hyksos, to seize the throne; a chain of fortresses and a connecting wall had been built to keep such hordes out, so that a sheik of Abram's weight arriving at that wall would be questioned by the Egyptian scribes and reported to the king. Clarke pursues the royal title instead, taking Pharaoh for the common appellation of the shepherd kings who had conquered the land, a word supposed to mean king in the old Egyptian tongue, though if the root be sought in Hebrew it yields the sense of being free or disengaged, which he thinks a name such freebooters might naturally assume. Henry reads the court itself with contempt, calling the princes who commended Sarai to their master pimps rather, and noting that they praised her not for what was really her praise, her virtue and modesty and faith, which were no excellencies in their eyes, but only for the beauty they thought too good for a subject.

Ellicott takes the presents as evidence of good faith rather than of purchase, since it was usual to give a woman's relatives a sum when taking her to wife, so that Pharaoh plainly believed himself to be acting lawfully, while the size of the gift shows that Sarai, in spite of her years, was reckoned a valuable acquisition. He also defends the list against a charge of inaccuracy, since asses were said not to be known in Egypt so early, yet they are represented on the tombs of Benihassan and were numerous as far back as the building of the pyramids; the horse, he observes, is absent. Clarke stops on the same list for a different reason, taking the chance to fix the vocabulary of the Pentateuch, and explains that the word for sheep comes from a root meaning to be plentiful, a proper term for eastern flocks that commonly bear twins and sometimes three or four, and that it covers goats as well, much as the Latin word covers small cattle in general. Gill reports what Egypt is said to have gained by the visit, since two heathen writers make Abram the teacher of astrology there.

Calvin finds the wording of the plague verse decisive: had Moses said only that God punished the king for adultery, it would not appear that Sarai's chastity had been cared for, but since he says plainly that the house was plagued because of Abram's wife, all doubt is removed, God having interposed in time to prevent the violation. Clarke and Wesley both admit they do not know what the plagues were, Clarke guessing from the parallel case that the women of the household were made barren, though he thinks the phrase implies more, and drawing the inference that Pharaoh understood them as marks of divine displeasure, so that some knowledge of the true religion survived in Egypt even then. Ellicott suggests a likelier deliverance, that a probation of some months preceded such a marriage and Sarai was probably saved by the formality, and calls Pharaoh's conduct upright and dignified. Calvin notices that no answer from Abram is recorded and thinks he may simply have assented to a just reproof, adding that he relapsed into the same fault later. Wesley draws the lesson from the rebuke, that good people too often suspect others beyond what there is cause for.
